title: Chesterton's fairyland
hook: Chesterton, in Orthodoxy (1908), argues life is a strange gift like a fairy tale

segments.voice: Yesterday, Soloviev, who longed for the churches of East and West to be one family again. Your line was all one.

Why is grass green? A small child asks, and the grown-up has an answer ready. Then the child asks why again, and again, until the grown-up runs out and says: it just is. The English writer G. K. Chesterton thought that last answer deserved a much longer look. In his book Orthodoxy there's a chapter called The Ethics of Elfland, and it starts in the nursery, with the fairy tales of his childhood. Those stories, he says, taught him something about the real world that grown-up books had missed.

In fairyland, nobody pretends a golden apple had to be golden. It's magic: someone chose it. Chesterton turns that around on the world outside the window. We call it a law that apples fall and leaves are green, and the word law makes it sound necessary, as if it couldn't have been any other way. But we don't actually know why it's this way and not another. A world where grass happens to be green is a world someone might have chosen. Then he goes a step further. We tend to think repetition means something is dead, like a machine. Chesterton suggests the opposite. A laughing child says "Do it again!" and means it every single time. Perhaps, he says, God makes each daisy separately and has never grown tired of making them, with the strength of a child who wants the same game over and over. Jesus pointed somewhere nearby: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." And the psalmist, looking out at creation, doesn't explain it at all. He marvels: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Chesterton's point isn't that the world is a fable. It's that the world is stranger than a fable, and that being alive at all is a gift nobody earned. And a gift, he says, leaves you wanting someone to thank.
screen: `FAIRYLAND: SOMEONE CHOSE IT` · `A LAW, OR A KIND OF MAGIC?` · `DO IT AGAIN` · `A GIFT WANTS SOMEONE TO THANK`

segments.voice: Pick one plain thing within reach, a spoon, a key, a slice of bread, and look at it as if you'd stepped into a story and this was the first one you'd ever seen: why this color, this shape, why here at all? Don't answer; let it be strange for a while. If you pray, you can borrow the psalmist's line: O Lord, how manifold are thy works.
Chesterton's fairyland. G. K. Chesterton's idea that the ordinary world is as strange and chosen as a fairy tale, and calls for thanks.
Your line: the world is strange. That closes a week of thinkers, from Wesley's warm heart to Chesterton's wonder. Day twelve sixty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Christians who love Chesterton often read Orthodoxy as a book of gratitude and wonder rather than argument alone; churches also give thanks for creation in their prayers, and some Christians say grace before meals.

chat.says: Chesterton and fairyland? Was he saying religion is just a fairy tale?
options: No. He said the real world is as strange as a fairy tale, and a gift that calls for thanks.
Yes. He said faith is a lovely story that grown-ups should keep just for the children.
No. He said fairy tales are harmful, and children should read only plain real facts.
chat.meaning: Chesterton said the world is stranger than a fable: grass might have been chosen green, and being alive is a gift that leaves you wanting to thank someone.
